Equal Protection. The equal protection clause, part of Section One of the Fourteenth Amendment ratified in 1868, prohibits states from denying any person the equal protection of the laws. This clause has become the constitutional foundation for striking down laws and government actions that discriminate on the basis of race, gender, national origin, and other suspect classifications. The Supreme Court has developed a multi-tiered framework to determine when government classifications violate equal protection.

The exact text states: nor shall any state deny to any person within its jurisdiction the equal protection of the laws. Part of the Fourteenth Amendment, it was ratified during Reconstruction to protect the rights of freed slaves. Importantly, it applies only to state action, not to purely private discrimination.

The Supreme Court uses three tiers of scrutiny. Strict scrutiny, the highest protection, applies to classifications based on race, national origin, and fundamental rights. The government must show a compelling interest and that the law is narrowly tailored to achieve it—and it almost always strikes down the law. Intermediate scrutiny applies to gender and other quasi-suspect classifications. The government must show an important governmental objective and that the classification is substantially related to that objective. Rational basis review, the lowest protection, applies to all other classifications. The law need only be rationally related to a legitimate government interest and is rarely struck down.

Key cases shaped this doctrine. Plessy v. Ferguson upheld separate but equal in 1896 before being overturned in 1954. Brown v. Board of Education struck down racial segregation in schools. Loving v. Virginia struck down miscegenation laws. Craig v. Boren established that gender classifications receive intermediate scrutiny. Modern applications have extended to racial discrimination, gender discrimination, disability discrimination, and discrimination based on sexual orientation and gender identity.
